idea.angle: Part 2 of our Jinn series (remind viewers of part 1 in one sentence). The most commonly reported jinn experiences in Turkey, centered on "karabasan" (the night-time pressing presence) and other widely reported patterns; use only documented, publicly reported accounts (news reports, published research, folklore archives), never invent names or cases. What witnesses describe, what the tradition says, and what sleep researchers say about sleep paralysis, without ruling on the faith. End by promising part 3 (similar encounters around the world).

script.title: Karabasan Sleep Paralysis: Why Your Room Turns Icy Cold
script.description:
Karabasan sleep paralysis affects millions across Turkey, but why do so many people wake up pinned under a crushing dark entity? In this investigation, we examine the night visits documented in Turkish folklore archives, classical Islamic texts, and modern neurology clinics to uncover why people wake up completely unable to move or breathe.

#karabasansleepparalysis #karabasan #sleepparalysis #turkishfolklore #islamicfolklore #jinn #remparalysis #hypnagogichallucination #nightterror #sleepdemon #beyondqaf

scenes.narration: You wake up in the middle of the night, fully conscious. But your mouth cannot make a sound, and your chest feels crushed under three hundred pounds, as heavy as a full-grown motorcycle sitting on your ribs. In Turkey, millions of people call this visitor karabasan sleep paralysis.
scenes.image_prompt: Medical graphic diagram of a person lying flat on a bed at midnight, showing a downward force arrow pressing three hundred pounds of weight directly onto the chest, set against a dark blue background.

scenes.narration: Almost every family across Turkey has at least one relative who swears this dark visitor pinned them down. Last week, we explored jinn, unseen beings described in ancient traditions as created from smokeless fire. Now, we examine why modern people claim this specific shadow sits on their chest and steals their breath.
scenes.image_prompt: Stylized graphic cross-section of a bedroom at night, showing a bed with a dark translucent human-shaped shadow leaning over the sleeper's torso, with blue lines indicating blocked airway flow.

scenes.narration: For generations, village elders warned that this visitor was a spirit that hunts people sleeping alone in dark rooms. But when university clinics in modern Turkish cities hooked sufferers up to brain monitors, they discovered something that surprised both doctors and elders. So what do people actually see when this strikes?
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic shot of a modern hospital sleep laboratory at night, with glowing computer monitors showing live brainwave charts next to a quiet observation room.

scenes.narration: The Turkish name tells you everything about what it feels like. Kara means black or dark, and basan means the presser, or the one that steps on you. It is not a monster hiding in the woods, but a shadow that waits until you lie helpless in bed.
scenes.image_prompt: Minimalist graphic diagram breaking down the Turkish word Karabasan into two parts: KARA meaning dark, and BASAN meaning the presser, in glowing blue lettering on dark stone.

scenes.narration: In folklore archives gathered by Turkish researchers over the past century, witnesses described this shadow almost identically. It usually looks like a heavy, faceless black shape hovering near the ceiling before dropping straight onto the sleeper's chest, sometimes wearing a small pointed hat made of wool.
scenes.image_prompt: Atmospheric shot of vintage folklore research notebooks and yellowed manuscript pages lying open on a dark oak desk under a warm lamp.

scenes.narration: Right before it lands, people report that the bedroom turns icy cold. A cozy bedroom heated to seventy degrees Fahrenheit suddenly feels freezing, like someone opened a window in the middle of winter, and the sleeper starts shivering right before their body locks up.
scenes.image_prompt: Graphic illustration of a bedroom temperature gauge dropping fast from seventy degrees Fahrenheit toward freezing, with cold blue thermal waves rolling over a sleeping figure.

scenes.narration: Next comes the silence. Victims try to scream for family members sleeping only ten feet away, about the length of a small car, but nothing comes out. Their vocal cords are completely frozen, as if someone pulled the plug between their brain and their throat.
scenes.image_prompt: Cutaway diagram of a human throat and vocal cords, showing silent sound waves blocked by bright red stop signs, explaining why no sound escapes.

scenes.narration: Medical surveys in Turkey show that over forty percent of college students report having this terrifying experience at least once. That is roughly four out of every ten young adults, nearly double the rate reported in Western Europe. That huge difference raises a big question: why does culture change how often our bodies freeze?
scenes.image_prompt: Clean bar chart infographic comparing forty percent of Turkish students on the left against twenty percent of Western European students on the right, in clean blue and white tones.

scenes.narration: In coastal villages along the Black Sea, grandmothers teach children strict rules to avoid the shadow. They warn you never to leave bread crumbs in your sheets, and never to sleep flat on your back, because lying face up leaves your chest open like a welcome mat.
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic twilight landscape of a misty wooden mountain village in northern Turkey, with blue dusk fog rolling over rustic rooftops.

scenes.narration: Village legends also claim that if you can grab the creature's felt hat while pinned down, it turns into pure gold and the creature must obey you. But in thousands of recorded accounts, not a single person ever managed to lift a single finger to touch it.
scenes.image_prompt: Conceptual graphic showing an antique wool felt hat floating in mid-air, with tiny gold particles falling from its brim against a pitch-black background.

scenes.narration: Many people assume that traditional Islam calls this creature a specific demon found in holy books. But that is completely wrong. The word karabasan never appears in the Quran or the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad; it is purely a folk word created by Turkish villagers over centuries.
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of an antique leather-bound book lying closed on dark velvet, lit gently by a single candle flame with deep shadows.

scenes.narration: However, Islamic texts do record traditions about unseen night disturbances during sleep. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in hadith number three thousand two hundred and ninety-five, the Prophet taught believers to wash out their nose three times upon waking, explaining that Satan stays in the upper nasal passage overnight.
scenes.image_prompt: Anatomical profile diagram of a sleeping human head showing the nasal passage, with traditional scholarly script and clean arrows indicating morning washing, in muted blues.

scenes.narration: In the thirteenth hundreds, a famous Islamic scholar named Ibn Qayyim wrote a medical book called Prophetic Medicine. He explained that choking during sleep has two possible causes: either physical fumes from bad digestion rising to the brain, or interference from unseen spirits.
scenes.image_prompt: Historical diagram of a two-way medical chart from the Middle Ages: one path labeled Body Gases rising to the head, and the other labeled Spiritual Disturbance, in clean scholar script.

scenes.narration: Three hundred years before that, around the year one thousand, the famous doctor Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, wrote about this same night terror in his Canon of Medicine. He called it al-kabus, meaning the nightmare that crushes, where a sleeper feels a heavy stone sitting on their ribs.
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of an ancient medical manuscript from the Islamic Golden Age, showing hand-drawn anatomical sketches of the lungs and windpipe on aged parchment.

scenes.narration: Ibn Sina treated it purely as a body problem, telling patients to eat lighter dinners, reduce worry, and stop sleeping on their backs. He was one of the first doctors in history to prove that this suffocating weight came from inside the human body, not from a demon outside.
scenes.image_prompt: Comparative medical diagram showing a human body sleeping flat on its back with blocked airways, next to a body resting comfortably on its side with open airways.

scenes.narration: Even so, religious scholars noticed that when terrified sleepers recite short holy verses, the crushing weight suddenly disappears. Sufferers say the exact second they recite verse two hundred and fifty-five of Surah al-Baqarah, known as Ayah al-Kursi, the shadow vanishes and they can move again. But does this happen because of faith, or because of brain chemistry?
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic shot of early morning light breaking through a stone arched window, driving away heavy midnight shadows from a simple bedroom.

scenes.narration: To find out, modern scientists put electrodes on patients' heads in sleep laboratories. They found that this crushing feeling happens during REM sleep, or rapid eye movement sleep, the stage of deep sleep when your brain makes intense dreams.
scenes.image_prompt: Clear medical diagram of a human brainstem sending chemical signals down the spinal cord to safely lock the arm and leg muscles during sleep.

scenes.narration: When you dream that you are running or falling, your brainstem releases two natural chemicals called glycine and GABA. These chemicals work like safety switches, temporarily paralyzing your arms and legs so you do not jump out of bed and hurt yourself.
scenes.image_prompt: Detailed illustration of brain cells releasing chemical messengers glycine and GABA, showing them locking nerve connections to keep muscles totally still.

scenes.narration: Normally, you wake up and your brain flips those safety switches back on instantly. But in sleep paralysis, your thinking mind wakes up while the body's chemical locks stay shut, leaving you trapped inside your own frozen body for thirty to one hundred and twenty seconds, about two minutes at most.
scenes.image_prompt: Timeline infographic showing a sixty-second timer bar between the mind waking up and the muscles unlocking, labeled with a thirty to one hundred and twenty second delay.

scenes.narration: Because your automatic breathing still works, your lungs keep pulling in air. But the muscles between your ribs, the ones you use to take a deep breath, are still paralyzed, making your chest feel like a heavy concrete block is sitting right on top of you.
scenes.image_prompt: Anatomical diagram of a human chest, showing the lower breathing muscle moving normally while the rib muscles stay frozen, creating the illusion of heavy weight.

scenes.narration: At the very same time, your brain's fear alarm, an almond-shaped part called the amygdala, goes into full panic. It realizes your body cannot move, assumes you are under deadly attack, and instantly projects dream monsters right into your dark bedroom.
scenes.image_prompt: Three-dimensional illustration of the human brain with the amygdala glowing in bright warning red, firing emergency alarm signals across the vision center.

scenes.narration: Your brain feels heavy pressure on your chest, so it invents a story to explain that pressure. In Turkey, people see a dark spirit called karabasan; in Canada, people see an old witch called the Old Hag; and in American cities, people often see an alien shadow standing by their bed.
scenes.image_prompt: World map diagram linking sleep paralysis myths: Karabasan in Turkey, the Old Hag in Newfoundland, and Shadow aliens in North America, each marked with clean icons.
scenes.chapter: The Cultural Link Between Mind and Myth

scenes.narration: This also explains why reciting a prayer or counting slowly helps people break free. Focusing on rhythmic words calms down your brain's fear center, giving your body the minute it needs to clear away those paralyzing chemicals.
scenes.image_prompt: Graph diagram showing a fast, spiking panic heart rate calming down into a steady, flat rhythm as calm mental focus takes over.

scenes.narration: In southeastern Turkey, doctors at Dicle University studied hundreds of patients and found that people who sleep less than six hours a night get karabasan three times more often. When you lose sleep, your brain gets confused and mixes your dreams directly into your waking life.
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic shot of a tired person sitting on the edge of a bed at night, rubbing exhausted eyes beside a glowing digital alarm clock showing 3:45 AM.

scenes.narration: How you lie down matters even more. Sleep doctors report that sleeping flat on your back makes you five times more likely to get paralyzed than sleeping on your side, because your tongue slips backward and partially blocks your breathing.
scenes.image_prompt: Medical comparison diagram: a sleeper flat on their back showing their tongue slipping back to block airflow labeled five times risk, next to a side sleeper with clear breathing.

scenes.narration: Amazingly, modern sleep advice matches Islamic teachings from fourteen hundred years ago. In Sahih Muslim, in hadith two thousand seven hundred and ten, the Prophet told believers to lie on their right side when going to sleep, which keeps your airways completely open.
scenes.image_prompt: Warm night shot of a sleeper resting comfortably on their right side on a simple mattress, lit by soft moonlight through a window.

scenes.narration: Still, many people in Turkey believe that science only explains part of the story. Doctors can explain how your muscles lock up, but they cannot explain why strangers with no connection describe the exact same dark figure glaring at them with pure hatred.
scenes.image_prompt: Conceptual graphic of a human head split in two: one side showing medical brainwaves, and the other side showing an ancient shadow figure, separated by a clean glowing line.
scenes.chapter: The Global Shadow and What Remains

scenes.narration: Anthropologists explain that when a community talks about an entity, the brain borrows that story whenever it panics. In Turkey, where elders talk about karabasan over tea, a scared teenager who wakes up paralyzed instantly imagines that exact creature.
scenes.image_prompt: Atmospheric evening shot of classic tulip-shaped Turkish tea glasses on an embroidered tablecloth, with steam rising under warm amber living room light.

scenes.narration: By contrast, in places where these old folk stories have been forgotten, people with the same muscle lock think they are having a heart attack or a stroke. The physical fear is identical everywhere, but the face you see comes from the stories you heard as a child.
scenes.image_prompt: Graphic layout showing three thought bubbles from a frozen sleeper: an ancient folklore monster, a hospital heart monitor, and a dark shadow silhouette.

scenes.narration: Traditional Islamic thought brings both views together. Scholars teach that unseen spiritual forces work through the physical laws of nature, meaning an unseen spirit could take advantage of your body when you are exhausted and your brain defenses are down.
scenes.image_prompt: Clean graphic of balanced scales in deep navy blue: one side holding a glowing diagram of brain chemistry, the other holding an ancient manuscript scroll.

scenes.narration: So whether this night terror is a quick chemical glitch in your brainstem or an unseen visitor, the practical advice is the same: take care of your body with good sleep habits, and say your prayers of protection before you close your eyes.
scenes.image_prompt: Peaceful nighttime bedroom bathed in soft moonlight, showing a sleeper resting quietly and safely on their side.

scenes.narration: Next week, in part three of our series, we leave Turkey and travel across the globe to see how this exact same crushing shadow appears in medieval European witch trials, Japanese ghost lore, and Native American legends. But what do you think is really happening in your bedroom?
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic shot of an antique brass globe slowly turning under library spotlighting, tracing ancient routes across Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia.

scenes.narration: When people wake up frozen in their beds, is it simply a temporary chemical glitch during dream sleep, or an encounter with an unseen presence from ancient tradition? Type one for brain chemistry, or type two for an unseen presence, in the comments below.
